theory.intro: A sample is **biased** when it does not fairly represent the population, so the result it gives is pushed away from the truth. Bias gets in through **who ends up in the sample** and through **how the questions are worded**. Diagnosing it means saying which group is left out or over-represented, or which words push the respondent towards an answer, then naming the bias and stating which way the result is distorted. Collecting more responses the same unfair way does not remove bias — it only repeats it.
facts: **Selection bias** — where, when or how the group was chosen makes it misrepresent the population (measuring the height of $15$-year-olds by surveying only the basketball team).
**Volunteer bias** — people decide for themselves whether to take part, so only those with a strong opinion or a special interest reply (a click-to-vote online poll).
**Survivorship bias** — only the cases that lasted or succeeded are in the data, and the failures are missing (judging a gym by its current members, when the unhappy ones have already quit).
**Small sample size** — too few people are asked to show the variety in the population (asking $3$ shoppers what a whole suburb wants).
**Leading question** — praise, emotional language or one-sided information pushes towards an answer ('Do you agree that this brilliant plan should go ahead?').
**Ambiguous question** — the wording can be read in more than one way, usually because a time period or a boundary is missing ('How often do you exercise?').
**Not enough choices** — the response options leave out answers people would give, such as a neutral or negative option, or they overlap so one value fits two boxes.
A **larger sample does not remove bias** — the same unfair selection is simply repeated more times.

foundation.question_text: A reporter wants to know what proportion of Australian adults have a full-time job. She surveys shoppers at a shopping centre at $11$ am on a Tuesday. Name the type of bias in this sample.
foundation.solution_text:
People with full-time jobs are at work at $11$ am on a Tuesday, so the place and time leave most of them out.
**Selection bias.**

foundation.question_text: A news website asks readers to click a link to vote on whether a new stadium should be built. Name the type of bias in this sample.
foundation.solution_text:
Only readers who choose to click take part, and those are the readers with the strongest opinions.
**Volunteer bias.**

foundation.question_text: A council asks $3$ shoppers at a shopping centre whether a new car park is needed, then reports that residents want one. Name the type of bias in this sample.
foundation.solution_text:
Three people cannot show the range of opinions held across a whole suburb.
**Small sample size.**

foundation.question_text: A gym measures how satisfied its members are by surveying only the people who currently hold a membership. Name the type of bias in this sample.
foundation.solution_text:
Members who were unhappy have already cancelled, so only the ones who stayed are left to be surveyed.
**Survivorship bias.**

foundation.question_text: A council asks the members of the local cycling club whether more cycle lanes should be built. Name the type of bias in this sample.
foundation.solution_text:
Cycling club members are far more likely to want cycle lanes than residents in general.
**Selection bias.**

foundation.question_text: A product-review form asks: 'How much did you enjoy our brilliant new blender?' Name the type of bias in this question.
foundation.solution_text:
The words 'brilliant' and 'enjoy' assume the customer liked the blender and push towards a positive answer.
**Leading question.**

foundation.question_text: A product-review form asks: 'How often do you use your blender?' Name the type of bias in this question.
foundation.solution_text:
No time period is given, so 'often' could mean per day, per week or per month, and different customers answer different questions.
**Ambiguous question.**

foundation.question_text: A product-review form asks customers to rate a blender, offering only the options **Good**, **Very good** and **Excellent**. Name the type of bias in this question.
foundation.solution_text:
A customer who disliked the blender has no option that fits, so every response recorded looks positive.
**Not enough choices.**

development.question_text: A video channel with $200\,000$ followers asks its followers whether its videos have improved this year. Explain why the sample is unrepresentative.
development.solution_text:
Followers already like the channel enough to follow it, and people who disliked the videos stopped watching and are never asked.
**The sample over-represents fans, so the responses will be more positive than the truth.**

development.question_text: A survey about how Australians travel to work is carried out in a shopping-centre car park. State one group that is left out, and say whether the proportion who drive will be over-estimated or under-estimated.
development.solution_text:
Everybody in a car park arrived by car, so people who catch a train, ride or walk are left out.
**The proportion who drive will be over-estimated.**

development.question_text: A running club emails a training survey only to the members who finished last year's marathon, asking whether the training program works. Name the bias, and describe one change that would fix it.
development.solution_text:
The members who withdrew or did not finish are missing, so only the successes are counted.
**Survivorship bias.**
The club should also survey the members who withdrew or did not finish, so the failures are included.

development.question_text: An online poll asks: 'Given that plastic bags are choking our oceans, should the shop charge for them?' Name the fault in the question, and rewrite it fairly.
development.solution_text:
The question supplies one-sided emotional information before asking, pushing the reader towards 'yes'.
**Leading question.**
A fair version is 'Should the shop charge for plastic bags?'

development.question_text: A product-review form asks how much a customer spent, offering the boxes \$0–\$10, \$10–\$20 and \$20–\$30. Explain why the responses will be unreliable.
development.solution_text:
The boxes overlap, so a customer who spent \$10 can tick either of the first two.
**The question is ambiguous, and two customers who spent the same amount can end up counted in different groups.**

development.question_text: A fitness app shows a pop-up asking users to rate it, and only the users who choose to reply do so. The app's users are all people who already exercise regularly. Name the bias that comes from **who chose to reply**, and explain it.
development.solution_text:
Users decide for themselves whether to answer the pop-up, so the ratings come only from users who felt strongly enough to reply.
**Volunteer bias.**
That every user already exercises regularly is a separate selection problem, not the bias asked for here.

development.question_text: A phone company measures how satisfied its customers are by surveying only its current customers. Name the type of bias, and state which way the satisfaction rating will be distorted.
development.solution_text:
Customers who were unhappy have already left the company, so only the ones who stayed are surveyed.
**Survivorship bias, and the satisfaction rating will be higher than the truth.**

mastery.question_text: A skateboard company reports that $96\%$ of the reviews on its website give its new deck $4$ stars or more. Only customers who registered the deck may leave a review, and the company deletes the reviews of customers who returned the deck for a refund. Name the bias created by **deleting the returned-deck reviews**, and explain why the $96\%$ cannot be used to claim that most buyers are happy.
mastery.solution_text:
The reviews come only from customers who kept the deck, because every customer who returned it has been deleted.
Only the cases that lasted are left in the data, which is **survivorship bias**.
The dissatisfied buyers are exactly the ones removed, so the $96\%$ describes only the buyers who were already happy and over-states satisfaction across all buyers.

mastery.question_text: An online poll asks: 'Given that the new stadium will cost \$800 million, do you agree that the money is wasted?' The only responses offered are **Agree** and **Strongly agree**. Identify two separate faults in this poll and explain the effect of each.
mastery.solution_text:
The question supplies one-sided cost information and then asks 'do you agree', which pushes the reader towards agreeing.
**Leading question.**
Both responses agree with the statement, so a reader who thinks the stadium is worth building cannot answer at all.
**Not enough choices.**
Together the two faults force an agreeing response, so the poll will report near-total agreement whatever readers actually think.

mastery.question_text: A club committee says its online poll cannot be biased, because $5000$ members responded. Explain why a large number of responses does not make the result unbiased, and describe a method that would.
mastery.solution_text:
All $5000$ responses came from members who chose to click the poll, so the same self-selected group is simply over-represented $5000$ times.
**Volunteer bias is not removed by collecting more of the same responses.**
Instead the committee should choose members from the full membership list and contact them directly, so that members who would never volunteer are still included.
